newsitem.title: USA: Gold stays under selling pressure.
newsitem.headline: Gold stays under selling pressure.

text.p: Gold revisited its 12-year low Wednesday as speculators remained edgy over the prospect of further gold sales by central banks.
On New York's Commodity Exchange, August gold tumbled $2.10 to close at $318.90 an ounce.
In London, bullion was fixed at $317.30 an ounce after falling to new 12-year low of $315.75 initially.
Despite the gloom, producers say physical demand for gold remains strong and they believe that the precious metal will recover.
Gold has been retreating since the Reserve Bank of Australia last Thursday said it had sold 167 metric tons of gold from its reserves over the past six months.

The announcement sparked heavy speculative selling on fears that other banks might also start to unload their gold. It also provoked criticism from the Australian gold mining industry, half of which is producing at a loss at current prices.
European central banks have been steady sellers of gold this past year to help their countries achieve the entry criteria for European Monetary Union in 1999.
"A European central bank selling would be one thing, but the central bank of the world's third-largest gold producer is even more bearish for the market," one analyst said.
Central bank gold reserves total more than 28,000 tons.
Producers believe that the actual announcement of Australia's gold sales rather than the extra supply has weighed on the market.

"We're going through a lot of pain right now but we need to look long-term," said Keith Spencer, general manager of Gold Fields of South Africa Ltd.'s gold operations. "There is a lot of negative sentiment about the Australian sales but the fall was triggered by the announcement. The market actually absorbed the gold sales," he said.
Spencer said physical demand for gold at the moment was the highest it has ever been.
According to Gold Fields Mineral Services, last year's gold demand, for jewelry, electronics and coins, was at 3,290 tons and total world supply stood at 3,490 tons.
Analysts said the giant South African gold industry is bracing for huge losses and layoffs of thousands of miners following the price plunge.
"It could be the worst thing the country has ever seen. This gold crisis is the last thing the country needs right now," said one analyst, who did not want to be identified.
South African mines are already digging deeper under the surface than any mines in the world to reach dwindling ore deposits, and the weakening prices could affect them severely.
Analysts expected the first bad signs to surface during the quarterly reporting season due to start on Thursday.
"I think we are going to see a bloodbath in general," said Angus Auchterlonie, an analyst for Mathison & Hollidge.
One exception might be Anglo American Corp. of South Africa Ltd., which could win some respite through its forward sales of gold.
South Africa's gold industry -- the world's largest producer, produced 495 tons of gold last year.
